text: Some lights save ships.
Some lights were built to drown them.
Previously, on the Keeper’s Island.
Every night at three twelve, the lamp went dark for twelve seconds, and a boat ran onto the north rocks.
The clues led under the headland, to a door older than the tower. And a stranger in a yellow coat who casts no shadow.
Three days were up. And Gus walked into the dark on purpose.
Mabel went first. Cats do not wait for permission.
Gus relit his lantern with a shaking match and followed her down.
Ninety-one steps. He counted every one.
At the bottom the tunnel opened, and the lantern light fell away into a space far too big to be inside an island.
Water, glowing green. A beach of black sand. Crates, rope, a jetty of old wood.
A harbour. Under the lighthouse. And the sand was full of fresh footprints.
On a stone block at the water’s edge stood something Gus knew better than his own face.
A lamp. Brass, lens, wick. A keeper’s lamp, smaller and older than his own.
He laid his hand on the glass.
It was warm.
Somebody had lit this lamp tonight, while the real one was dark.
And its lens was not pointed at the sky. It faced a crack in the rock, a slit that opened onto the sea…
straight at the north rocks.
At sunrise Pip was sent out with one job. Find where that light comes out.
He circled the north cliff eleven times, mostly to be admired.
On the twelfth, he saw it. A slit in the rock just above the waterline, black, the width of a door.
From out at sea, a light in there would sit low and steady. Right below the lighthouse.
Gus went very quiet. Every keeper knows what two lights, one above the other, mean to a sailor.
They mean: line us up, and you are safe.
Old Wren did not look surprised. She looked like someone who had been waiting sixty years for this visit.
Before the tower, this island had wreckers. A false light on a stormy night, and the sea brought them a ship.
They kept a ledger of every wreck. And every name that lit the lamp.
She opened it at the last page. One line, sixty years old, in careful, familiar handwriting.
It was his grandfather’s.
Gus never knew his mother. He knew a photograph, a yellow coat on a hook, and one sentence everyone on the island repeated.
She rowed out into the storm the night you were born, and the sea kept her.
He had kept the lamp lit for thirty years so the sea would never keep anyone else.
Three o’clock. Gus, Mabel, and Rollo, who had insisted, crouched behind the crates.
The lantern was turned down to a bead. Nobody breathed loudly. Rollo had brought snacks.
Three eleven. The water moved.
Something rose out of it. A hood. Shoulders. A yellow coat, streaming wet, walking up the shelf as if the sea were a staircase.
Three twelve. Far above, the real lamp went dark.
And down here, the stranger lit the other one.
The stranger stood by the lamp and counted. Gus could see the hood move. One. Two. Three.
Nine seconds in, Rollo sneezed.
The hood turned. Not toward the noise. Toward Gus. As if the stranger had known all along exactly where he was.
Then a splash, a ring of green light on the water, and nothing.
Rollo, ashamed, ran to the waterline to make up for it. He came back dragging something on a chain.
A silver locket. Inside, a tiny painted face Gus had only ever seen in his mother’s photographs.
His own. As a baby.
Gus put the locket on Dunn’s desk and said nothing. It worked better than shouting.
Dunn sighed, unlocked a drawer, and took out the wrecked boat’s registry plate.
No owner. No port. No crew. Just a name painted on the bow.
She was called the Keeper’s Daughter.
Gus never had a sister. His mother was the keeper’s only daughter.
And she was lost at sea the night he was born.
Marlo runs the ferry. She is twenty-two, she has crossed this water four thousand times, and nobody on the council has ever asked her a thing.
That night I was out late. I saw the lamp go dark. Twelve seconds. Then I saw the other one.
Low, by the water. Steady. And that boat turned toward it like it had been told to.
Two lights. One high, one low. Gus closed his eyes and saw the whole thing at once.
Pause here. Two lights, one above the other. A boat that steered onto the rocks as if it had been told to.
You already know how sailors use two lights. Think about what happens when one of them moves.
Here is the trick. A ship coming home lines up two lights, one behind and above the other.
When the high light sits right on top of the low one, you are in the safe channel. Every sailor knows it.
But move the low light, and the safe line moves with it. Put it in the cliff, and the line runs straight onto the north rocks.
And if the high lamp goes dark for twelve seconds, a sailor has only one light left to trust.
Whoever did this was no wrecker. Only a keeper knows the lamp that well.
Back in the cave, Gus tried his own lamp key in the old brass door. It turned like it had been waiting.
Two locks. Two keys. One for the lamp above, one for the lamp below.
The second key, said the island, had always lived in the post office safe.
Wren opened the safe without being asked.
Empty. A clean square in the dust where a key had lain for sixty years.
I know who has it, Gus. I gave it to her myself.
That night Gus slept for the first time in a week. Mabel and Rollo took the watch.
Rollo watched the lamp. Mabel watched the sea. And just before dawn, Mabel’s ears went flat.
Far out, past the north rocks, a small light was moving. Toward the island. In no hurry at all.
They sat in the sun outside the post office, and for a long time Wren just held the locket.
The night you were born, a ship hit the rocks. Your mother rowed out to it alone. She never came back.
Except she did, Gus. This autumn. She came to my door in a yellow coat, and asked me for the key.
Gus had spent his whole life keeping a light for a mother he thought the sea had taken.
The sea had given her back. And she had come home to put the light out.
The storm came in at midnight. At three, through the rain, a ship’s lights. A real ferry, full of passengers, coming home.
At three eleven, Gus watched the top lamp flicker.
He could run up ninety-one steps to the tower, or down ninety-one steps to the cave.
Twelve seconds. One staircase.
He chose down.
She was there, by the low lamp, hand on the shutter, watching the ship come on through the crack.
Gus did not shout. He set his lantern down on the sand.
You kept it lit, little one. Sixty years. I watched you every night.
The sea has my debt. A ship for every year it gave me. Four ships. Then I am free.
Gus put his hand on the hot shutter, next to hers.
Then the man who has never let a light go out, closed one.
Thirty-one passengers walked off the ferry at dawn and never knew how close they had come.
Marlo knew. She waved at the lighthouse until her arm hurt.
On the north rocks, Gus found the yellow coat, folded neatly, a stone on top so the wind would not take it.
Under the stone, the brass key. And a fourth mark, freshly burned into the rock.
Four marks. Three ships. The sea was still owed one.
And Gus had just taken away the only person who knew how to pay it.
One more question before the end. The tale said four marks, one for each year the sea let him live.
The stranger said four ships. Count the wrecks you have seen, and count the marks.
That night the lamp turned, and turned, and did not miss once.
But at three twelve, far out at sea, a horn answered it. From somewhere no ship should be.
